nameStory: The striped burrfish gets its name from two distinctive behaviors and features. The 'striped' part comes from the dark bands that wrap around its round body like a zebra's markings. The 'burrfish' name refers to its ability to wedge itself into tight spaces in rocks and coral when threatened, plus the sharp spines covering its body that stick out like burrs on clothing.
description: The striped burrfish is a small, round pufferfish with a body covered in short, sharp spines that feel like coarse sandpaper. It typically grows to about 6-10 inches long and has a balloon-like shape that becomes even rounder when it puffs up with water or air when scared. Dark vertical stripes wrap around its tan to yellowish body, and it has large, prominent eyes that can move independently. Unlike some pufferfish, its spines are always visible rather than hidden under the skin.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Round, balloon-like body that feels firm and slightly rough to the touch, capable of inflating into an even rounder ball when threatened

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Short, sharp spines covering the entire body that are always visible and feel like coarse sandpaper or small thorns when touched gently

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Distinctive dark brown or black vertical stripes wrapping around a tan, yellow, or pale body, creating a banded appearance

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, bulging eyes that can move independently of each other, positioned high on the head

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish typically 6-10 inches long, fitting comfortably in cupped hands when not inflated

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in shallow coastal waters around rocky areas, jetties, and eelgrass beds where it can hide in crevices

habitat: In New England, striped burrfish inhabit shallow coastal waters, typically found around rocky jetties, breakwaters, and areas with eelgrass beds. They prefer areas with plenty of hiding spots like rock crevices and underwater structures in depths from just below the surface to about 30 feet. These fish are more common in the warmer southern New England waters, especially around Cape Cod and the islands.

seasonality.spring: Striped burrfish begin moving into New England waters as temperatures warm, becoming more active in shallow areas as they search for food.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for spotting burrfish, when they're most active and visible in shallow waters around docks and rocky areas. This is when they're easiest to observe and photograph.
seasonality.fall: Still present but beginning to move to deeper waters or migrate south as temperatures drop. Their activity decreases noticeably in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters during winter months, as most individuals move south or into deeper, warmer waters offshore.

funFact: When a striped burrfish inflates itself into a spiky balloon, it becomes virtually impossible for predators to swallow – but it also can't swim properly and must float helplessly at the surface until it deflates, making this defense a last resort that leaves them completely vulnerable to being scooped up by birds or curious humans!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with northern puffers, but striped burrfish always have visible spines (like a spiky golf ball) while puffers have smooth skin. Remember: if you can see and feel spines even when the fish is relaxed, it's a burrfish; if the skin feels smooth, it's a puffer.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'burrfish,' this species doesn't actually burrow in sand like some fish. The name is misleading – they get into tight spaces between rocks but don't dig. Also, like other pufferfish family members, they can be toxic if eaten, so they're strictly a look-but-don't-eat species.
compareHints: The striped burrfish is the only member of its genus found in New England waters. Compared to other porcupinefish family members like the porcupinefish itself, the striped burrfish is much smaller and has shorter, always-visible spines rather than long spines that lie flat until the fish inflates. Its stripes are also more regular and vertical compared to the more mottled patterns of its relatives.
